rv.q: With a delicacy that belies its crude vocabulary, “reasons to be pretty” celebrates the everyday heroism in the struggle to find out.
LaBute's dialogue crackles with authenticity, capturing the rhythms of blue-collar speech with an ear that's both accurate and theatrical.

The complicated, often explosive relationships between men and women are a source of eternal, often contrary fascination for Neil LaBute, and they have been superbly realized in 'Reasons to Be Pretty,' his most compassionate, appealing work to date.

"Playwright/provocateur Neil LaBute has explored our obsession with physical appearance and the way it wreaks havoc on relationships in such works as "Fat Pig" and "The Shape of Things." But "reasons to be pretty," the third entry in this unofficial trilogy, cuts even deeper than its predecessors.

It takes a tender man to make plays as tough as Neil LaBute's. No contemporary writer has more astutely captured the brutality in everyday conversation and behavior; that kind of insight requires sensitivity and soul-searching.
"Reasons to Be Happy" has its improbabilities and rough edges, but what ultimately emerges is a winning sympathy for the difficulties of life and love.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actress in a Play

cn.t: LaBute's most compassionate work to date cuts deep with a lacerating yet funny exploration of beauty and relationships. Critics find this taut drama unexpectedly affecting, praising its thoughtful meditation on self-worth and cruel communication.

vs.sum: The Lyceum Theatre offers good sightlines and a charming Beaux Arts ambiance, but suffers from cramped seating and small restrooms. Ideal for intimate dramas, but patrons should be prepared for less comfort during their visit.

acc.note: 4 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. No elevator. Infrared devices available.
